claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially a high-temperature BCC phase.
The initial high-temperature BCC phase has a uniform elemental distribution.
Local chemical segregation develops during cooling from the high-temperature BCC state.
Al is a principal segregating element during cooling.
Cooling-induced compositional heterogeneities govern subsequent nucleation and growth of secondary phases during thermal exposure.
Slow cooling permits differential diffusion and elemental segregation.
Rapid quenching minimizes diffusion and segregation.
Differences in elemental diffusivities during slow cooling generate local compositional fluctuations.
Al diffuses sufficiently during slow cooling to produce enrichment or depletion in local regions.
The cooling-induced compositional fluctuations lower the nucleation barrier for intermetallic or ordered secondary phases.
Rapid quenching preserves a homogeneous BCC state through the subsequent thermal exposure.
Slowly cooled samples will have more detectable local segregation, particularly of Al, than rapidly quenched samples.
After identical thermal exposure, slowly cooled samples will form a greater extent of secondary phases than rapidly quenched samples.
Rapidly quenched baseline samples will remain largely BCC after thermal exposure.
The proposed mechanism applies only when cooling and exposure conditions permit the required diffusional processes.
